patches.old_english:
**[Continuation of al-Mahāʾimī from p. 149]**: These reflected forms are subordinate, in their order, to the original form that is known in itself.

**Qūnawī:** Thus there arises a fresh knowledge of the kinds of manifestation and the rulings necessarily accompanying them. These rulings comprise the effects of things upon one another, whether through establishing or undoing, outwardly or inwardly, in higher or lower realms, within a determinate duration or without such duration, and in concordance or in discordance. All of this occurs through the connection brought about among them by the existential, immediately experienced self-disclosure, which gathers their dispersed elements together, as we explained.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** When the many determinate things make the One appear manifold in the kinds of manifestation proper to their various receptive capacities, the forms in which the One appears also differ. Accordingly, knowledge of those kinds of manifestation is said to be renewed, meaning that it follows knowledge of unity by an order of nature, not by a temporal succession. The manifested reality and the locus in which it is manifested are united with respect to existence; the manifest form is, in truth, that very reality, while its otherness concerns its status as an image. Therefore knowledge of the image follows knowledge of essential unity in rank.

These manifestations have determinate consequences. Something may affect another by bringing something about, as rain causes a crop to grow, or by undoing it, as fire burns wood. Such relations may be outward, as in those physical examples, or inward, as when two affirmative premises yield an affirmative conclusion and premises including a negative yield a negative conclusion. They may belong to higher orders, as with the influence of intellects upon souls and what lies below them, or to lower orders, as with the generation and corruption of elements acting upon one another. They may be time-bound, as in effects of intellects upon elements or elements upon one another, or not time-bound, as in the influence of intellects upon souls. They may be concordant, as good actions conduce to felicity, or discordant, as corrupt actions bring misery and punishment.

All these are diverse knowledges and are said to be renewed only in the sense that their order depends on the judgment of unity and the connection among the things themselves. Even when the things are contrary to one another, they are joined by the one existential disclosure common to them all, within eternal knowledge. What changes is the relational determination between that knowledge and the things, in view of the contrarieties belonging to them. Understand this carefully.

**Qūnawī:** Knowledge, delight and felicity, in all their different varieties, are in proportion to *munāsaba*—correspondence or affinity—while ignorance, pain and wretchedness are in proportion to the strength of the rulings of separation and distinction. Where the rulings of union are mingled with those of distinction, their relative dominance is displayed. The origin of each cluster of these rulings in a particular kind of affinity, and the point to which it returns as a relation, is what is called a *martaba*, a rank or level. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If the highest degree of knowledge of a thing is union with the known, then knowledge of all degrees, together with the enjoyment and felicity corresponding to it, follows the degree of correspondence between knower and known, between the one enjoying and what is enjoyed, and between the felicitous person and what confers felicity. Gnosis, faith, virtuous character and good deeds bring about this correspondence. Conversely, ignorance, torment and misery occur according to the strength of the differences separating the ignorant person from what is unknown, the sufferer from what causes suffering, and the wretched person from what makes him wretched. One must therefore avoid unbelief, vicious dispositions and disobedience, lest these rulings of separation and difference predominate.

Separation has these effects because it opposes correspondence and therefore yields contrary effects. Where it is weak, it cannot overcome the original correspondence arising from the participation of all things in existence. But where the rulings of union—associated with the attributes of necessity—and those of separation—associated with the attributes of possibility—are mixed in approximately equal strength, each exercises its sway for as long as the mixture lasts. A person in whom both are present may be knowing, happy and enjoying under one aspect but not under another. Thus the people of the Paradise of Acts are felicitous insofar as they are delivered from the Fire, yet deficient in felicity relative to the people of the Paradises of the Attributes and of the Essence.

Someone who first enters the Fire and later Paradise is, on this account, governed at first by separation and afterwards by union. The power of faith belongs to the person's inward spirit, while the power of bad acts attaches to outward behaviour. What attaches to the outward can pass away, unlike what is rooted in the inward. It is also possible to state the governing principle more simply: ignorance, torment and misery arise only where separation and distinction become strong, for when weak they cannot defeat the original affinity of existence.

Nor should one imagine that union abolishes all distinction. Both determinations persist after manifestation: under the consideration of necessity there is the One, necessary Reality, present throughout; under the consideration of determinations and possible attributes there are always creatures. The origin of each cluster of the rulings of union and of distinction, through a particular affinity with real unity, is what is designated a rank (*martaba*).

**[Continuation of al-Mahāʾimī]**: God therefore knows all such things perfectly, and correspondence has an effect on them from His side, for in Him it is primordial. Their correspondence, however, does not make them attain that same knowledge, because it is derivative and weaker. Affinity may be common to two terms, but its power differs according to the rank of each. What the relationship between God and creation, or creation and God, ultimately refers to is precisely this rank. Its operation at the level of God, whose unity is original, is incomparably greater than at the level of creatures, whose unity is derivative through existence. Without this distinction, the two knowledges would be equal merely because both parties share a correspondence. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** When I began composing this text, I was told inwardly, in the course of writing, that the rulings attributed to unity and to the one Real, expressed as the rulings of necessity, have, as viewed from unity, a single foundational ruling: the reality of *qaḍāʾ* (decree). The *maqādīr* (measures) are the effect of the manifold determinations of the objects of knowledge relative to that single ruling. The appearance of existence in accordance with those differentiations involves first a reception of influence and then an exercise of influence among the enumerated things, by restoring to them the effects proper to them. Know this, consider the strange matter to which I have drawn attention, and you will attain a rare knowledge. God is the guide.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This expands the explanation of the perfection of divine knowledge in both its undifferentiated and detailed aspects. The former is called decree; the latter, measure or determination, without excluding either from the comprehensiveness of the divine Essence. The rulings attributed to unity—namely the first determination—and to the One Real—namely the second determination or degree of divinity—are called rulings of necessity. But their ultimate origin, when viewed from unity, is one ruling: the reality of decree, or the divine knowledge of His Essence in His Essence. In the degree of the first determination, these rulings are not actually multiple, so union with the objects of knowledge is most intense there. This is why one is obliged to accept the decree with contentment.

As for the measured determinations, their meaning is that each object of knowledge occurs in its apportioned measure of time, place and accompanying accidents. At any given moment the knower receives from the absolute Essence a new determination appropriate to the state of the recipient, distinct from what was delimited previously. **[Continuation of the discussion of Text Thirteen]**

**Qūnawī:** By contrast, the Real displays Himself through states, as the Most High says, “Every day He is upon some affair” (Qurʾān 55:29). Understand; do not interpret the matter away. Endeavour instead first to see it directly. Believe, submit, and you will be safe. God alone gives success and inspiration.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Human states do not reach a final state after which none is possible. Their change and succession is a matter of observation. Since they are determinations of the absolute Essence and varieties in the appearances of that Essence, the Real's determinations and modes of disclosure to human beings have no final limit. A determination differs from a variety of manifestation: the former is a cause of manifestation insofar as it is surrounded by the qualifying attributes that bring the manifestation about; the latter is the diversity of appearances occasioned by diverse determinations. Because human states and attributes constitute loci in which the Essence appears under the consideration of attributes, their diversity occasions diversity of manifestation, and each manifestation entails a determinate relation of correspondence. Human states thus serve as qualifying conditions for such differentiations. The divine names, under which the Real becomes determined, are names in relation to those human states, which mediate the diversity of manifestation and hence of determinations.

The Qurʾānic statement that He is engaged in an affair each day (55:29) has elsewhere been used to indicate that these affairs are inexhaustible: the days do not terminate, so neither do the affairs. Since the divine affairs stand in relation to the fixed entities and the comprehensive human being includes all of these, the states of the human being are likewise inexhaustible, as are the resulting varieties of manifestation and determinations. It is therefore impossible to encompass them. How, then, could one reach their furthest end and proceed beyond them to circumscribe what lies beyond? Understand. Do not reinterpret this statement away, for it is intended as stated; seek to witness it. Believe first and submit, rather than mistakenly claim to know what cannot be known, namely the Real through every one of His determinations. God grants this realization, which is the realization of the limits of knowing; He inspires surrender where attainment has been found impossible. God knows best.

**[Opening of Text Fourteen, on the same printed page.] Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī designates the following text an exalted text. The preceding discussion established that the Real is united with all things, and therefore knows them perfectly, whereas creatures cannot be united with Him in the same fashion and so cannot know Him through all His determinations, much less in absolute freedom from determination. The present text explains the majesty that both permits and veils this union. Under unconditioned absoluteness, unity so prevails that multiplicity does not appear, even though the absolute has a relation to determination. **Qūnawī:** Know that no existent described as absolute lacks an aspect toward restriction, even if only through becoming a determinate object of the thought of some thinker or several thinkers. The least restriction is that the absolute becomes distinguished as an object in someone's understanding. The conception of a thing requires that it be represented through a likeness by which it is distinguished from other things, whether essentially or accidentally, even at the level of a single instance. Equally, anything judged to be restricted has an aspect toward absoluteness. One cannot make a judgment about the absolute without recognizing some character under which to judge it; once recognized, the character may form the apparent limitation. Yet it still has an aspect toward the absolute, because a limiting predicate inheres in something more fundamental than that predicate, to which thought can return. The bearer cannot simply be eliminated while the predicate remains, for an attribute cannot subsist without a subject. Hence the existence in every conditioned existent is the absolute, intrinsically necessary existence of the Real, which is qualified by the attributes of its loci of appearance.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The perfection inseparable from the Real may be considered in three ways. In the first, it is divided into intrinsic and nominal perfection. Intrinsic perfection is that whose existence and manifestation depend on nothing: it is eternally and perpetually manifest to the Essence in the Essence, without dependence on determinations or restrictions, for the Real is independent of all worlds. The existence of nominal perfection, on the other hand, likewise depends on nothing, but its manifestation and actual expression depend on the world's coming to exist, because the names express relations between Essence and things and a relation is not manifested without its terms. This does not mean that the Essence gains a perfection it lacked; rather, after its perfect manifestation to itself, it manifests within distinct loci.

Under a second consideration, both are perfections of the names: to judge that the Real possesses perfection, one must first conceive what is being judged. Such a conception distinguishes the subject from what lies outside it, however slightly—even, for example, through our conceiving it before the names are attributed to it or through our distinguishing its independence in the possession of existence. Anything distinguished in relation to something else is in that respect determined. Every determination through which the Real is conceived is called a divine name among the realizers, for names are, considered as bare relations, non-existent in themselves and cannot be independent causes of existence. **[Text Sixteen, after the introduction translated on p. 160.]**

**Qūnawī:** The reality of the Real consists of the form of His knowledge of Himself, inasmuch as that knowledge is determined through its relation to Himself, under the consideration in which knowledge, the knower and the known are one.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** What essentially distinguishes the Real from everything else is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Were such a form hypothetically distinct from what it represents, it would correspond perfectly to it. Here, however, the point is the necessary self-relation of knowledge entailed by His conception of Himself. This excludes consideration of God's self-knowledge through His appearance in the loci of manifestation, or through the conception other knowers possess of Him. Nor does His knowledge of Himself involve an added intelligible image standing over against a separately existing subject, with another relation joining them. Such an image would veil the known, and God is exalted above this. It would also introduce multiplicity into the first determination, which is simple from every point of view. Rather, knowing, knower and known are one, because neither the image nor its relation adds something to what is imaged. This excludes the differentiated self-knowledge ascribed under the degree of the names.

**Qūnawī:** His intrinsic attribute, which is not other than His Essence, is a unicity of comprehensiveness—an all-gathering oneness beyond which no gathering, relation or consideration can be conceived.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī mentions the intrinsic attribute because it is through such an attribute that the Essence is known to the highest degree available to the knower. It is not other than the Essence in what it refers to, even if the concepts of subject and attribute differ. Without conceptual difference there could be no meaningful predication of an attribute of a subject. The intrinsic attribute is the unique comprehension of existence and all its ranks and descriptions. Nothing more comprehensive can be conceived, for it comprehends both unity as distinguished from differentiation and unity as gathering differentiation, without either opposing the other or restricting the comprehensiveness to one side. There is no special relation confining it to gathering rather than differentiation, nor an unqualified absoluteness superadded to it as a further consideration. It comprehends both the unrestricted and the conditioned without being confined by the very description of comprehending them.

**Qūnawī:** A noble text.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In the preceding text it was said that all things subsist in the Real, although the Eternal cannot be the receptive locus of originated events. Earlier, it had been said that the Real pervades all things, although the Eternal is too exalted to be contained in the originated. This noble text removes that apparent difficulty, since it explains how something originated may be described as eternal under one consideration, and how the Eternal may be described as newly appearing under another. The preceding statement, that every absolute reality has an aspect toward determination and vice versa, is not thereby overturned.

**Qūnawī:** The manner in which anything is in something else follows the character of its locus, whether that locus is intelligible or formal. Consequently, the possible objects of knowledge, insofar as their determinations are established and inscribed in the knowledge of the Real, are described as pre-eternal. Likewise, everything determined in divine knowledge bears, under another aspect, the ruling of origination: the existence of the world and the knowledge possessed by its inhabitants are originated and receptive, unlike the existence and knowledge of the Real. Know this, and, if God wills, you will be rightly guided.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The establishment of any state in a locus is qualified as originated or pre-eternal in accordance with the locus, even if considered in itself that state would not be so qualified. This is true whether the locus is intelligible, such as the Creator's knowledge or created intellects, or formal, as in elemental bodies.

The possible objects of knowledge are originated by their own nature. Nevertheless, they are described as pre-eternal insofar as their determinations subsist in the eternal divine knowledge: what is established in that knowledge as an object of knowledge is not something temporally superadded to it. One must not make divine knowledge a place in which new events come to be. The same determined objects, which are described as eternal insofar as they are known by God, are subject to the ruling of origination insofar as they exist externally. The being of the cosmos and the knowledge of its inhabitants are originated in their outward existence, for they are receptive of and dependent on God's existence and knowledge.

This is not the case with the existence and knowledge of the Real, which are eternal considered in themselves. When originated things appear, the ancient existence and knowledge may be described as newly appearing **with respect to manifestation and relation**, not through an origination in themselves. The Eternal is related to the originated and thus receives a relative description without changing in His own reality. Understand this and you will reconcile the outward law (*sharīʿa*) and the inner reality (*ḥaqīqa*) at the point from which pure divine unity proceeds, if God wills.

**Qūnawī:** A noble text, among the noblest, most majestic and most comprehensive statements of the universal principles of divine and cosmic knowledge.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding text examined a thing under the aspect of the locus in which it is established; the present text considers what belongs to it under the aspect of itself. It discusses the divine realities: the Essence, its essential names and their rulings, its essential efficacy and being effective, its knowledge and its unity; the way its knowledge acts as a mirror of the Essence and names and as the source of multiplicity; and the ranks, their relations and the arising of some from others. The text is noble because it gathers the results of the previous texts, majestic because it includes their premises, and comprehensive because it unites beginnings and ends.

**Qūnawī:** Know that the application of the name *Essence* (*dhāt*) is true of the Real only in respect of His determination: that first determination which, in the conception of creatures other than the perfected, comes after an imagined absoluteness whose nature is unknown and which has no name. That supposed absoluteness is a negative description of the Essence, imagined as distinct from every determination. The affirmative reality actually given, however, is the first determination.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Beginners in this discipline sometimes suppose that the name *Essence* belongs to the Real under the aspect of sheer absoluteness. But this absoluteness is a negative meaning, without a known attribute or a name. They call it the unseen of the Real because, according to their supposition, it stands above everything. If *Essence* named something below this absoluteness, the absoluteness would be above the divine Essence; yet all agree that nothing is above Him.

The supposition derives from the reasoning that every determination is preceded by non-determination, and that non-determination is absoluteness. Qūnawī corrects it. The word *Essence* signifies the Real under consideration of the first determination, since there is, by agreement, no name preceding it. To make *Essence* the name of something prior to that determination contradicts the very assertion that the supposed prior absoluteness is not circumscribed by being an essence, just as it is not circumscribed by any description. Moreover, the Real's intelligible determination in His knowledge of Himself is considered at the first determination: what has not been conceived under that aspect by the Real cannot be conceived as something superordinate by another knower, so that the name *Essence* could be applied to it.

What the unperfected understand as a prior absoluteness is thus a mental supposition formed by contrast with various modes of absoluteness and restriction. It is a negative description, not another entity higher than the Real. Something can stand above another only if it is itself something. If one objects that it must be something because it is distinguished from all determination, the answer is that the distinction is imposed by imagination; it places an imagined non-determination above every real determination. [The argument continues on p. 168.]

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Non-determination is a negative consideration and therefore cannot genuinely be above or prior to what is determined. The first determination alone is the affirmative reality at issue. Accordingly, *the divine Essence* is a name applied there, not a name for a non-existent abstraction. Certainly one may describe the Essence negatively as not confined by either absoluteness or restriction. That is an account relative to the ranks, not an additional state prior to the first determination. Because it commonly figures in ordinary people's conception, they imagine it to precede that first determination. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** The Essence intrinsically comprehends the essential names, the keys of the unseen; and the referent of the name *Essence* is in no respect other than its names. The names, however, differ from and oppose one another; and again they are united with one another from the standpoint of the Essence that comprehends them all.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The first determination intrinsically includes the essential names, the keys of the unseen and of the divine relations: the Living, the Knowing, the Powerful, the Willing, the Hearing, the Seeing and the Speaking. Were these names present only through a further intermediary, that intermediary, rather than the essential names themselves, would be the key of the unseen.

An objection might be raised: if the first determination included several names, it would no longer be the first determination but already the presence of the names. The answer is that in the first presence the One named by the term *Essence* differs in no respect from His names. In their own presence, the second determination, the names differ conceptually from one another, sometimes oppose one another in their rulings, and also agree in the comprehending Essence. Thus they may be predicated of one another in one respect and all of them predicated of the Essence. Unity at the first determination is not equivalent to the abolition of the names; nor is their differentiation at the second equivalent to a plurality of independent essences.

**Qūnawī:** Unicity (*aḥadiyya*) describes the determination, not an absolutely unqualified something supposed to be determined, since what is absolutely unqualified has no name and no attribute.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This anticipates an objection. How can the Essence include the essential realities expressed by the names if it is called *Essence* at its first determination, when only the Essence alone can be conceived? Is it not called unicity precisely because the names are not distinguished there? How, then, can it comprehend them under that aspect?

Qūnawī's reply is that absolute indetermination, as such, does not become determined and has neither name nor attribute. Hence it cannot itself be described as determination or unicity. In the consideration of *aḥadiyya* the names are not distinguished; in that of *wāḥidiyya* the names are taken into account. Yet the Essence is more comprehensive than the descriptions of it as either unicity or unitive plurality, and can therefore comprehend the names without their becoming separately distinguished in the first consideration. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** From the standpoint of these names, insofar as the Essence does not differ from them, we say that the Real acts by the Essence. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This follows from the names' non-otherness in relation to the Essence. The realized knowers can therefore say that the Essence effects things without an intermediary. On the other hand, the Essence considered solely in itself is self-sufficient beyond the worlds, so the operation of the names must also be acknowledged. Yet those names are the very Essence at the rank of unicity, and are included by the Essence at the rank of *wāḥidiyya*. Under the former respect and in their actual referent, what appears to be an intermediary is not a second entity standing between the Essence and its effect. Qūnawī's injunction to understand indicates that those who speak of an intermediary also speak truly, but under a different consideration.

**Qūnawī:** The Essence has just one inseparable concomitant, different from it only relationally; that concomitant is knowledge.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Consider the seven essential names. The Essence has one first concomitant, whether approached under the aspect of *aḥadiyya* or of *wāḥidiyya*; the others follow through it, in the order of intelligible dependence. Even this first concomitant is not really separate from the Essence. Under the differentiated aspect of *wāḥidiyya* it is distinct only by relation, and under unicity the knower, knowledge and known are united from every aspect. Thus what might be spoken of as an intermediary between Essence and the other essential names is not an intermediary in any fully independent sense.

Qūnawī specifies *knowledge*, rather than *life*, as the immediate concomitant. Knowledge conceptually presupposes life, but life is itself cognized through knowledge. The dependence in view is therefore one of conception rather than temporal production. [Continued p. 170.]

**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...they do not exercise an effect independently, but only through existence. Such too is the relation of the rulings of necessity to the ranks: these rulings are effective, and their effects appear in all that is related to a rank and becomes determined there, through the conditioning of unrestricted effusion as it reaches and passes through the rank.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The text explicitly repeats that it is **the ranks**, not the previously mentioned names, that have fixed entities, lest the pronoun be taken as referring to the nearest antecedent. Their mode of efficacy is that of intelligible loci of the combined rulings of necessity and possibility. The fixed entities considered as intelligible forms are, under that respect, non-existent externally; the non-existent does not act upon what exists. The qualified effusion, however, is existential and realized externally. Thus the fixed entities possess no independent power to produce it. Their effect is through existence, which carries the rulings of necessity through the essential names, and the rulings of possibility through the derivative names.

Why, then, does Qūnawī not simply attribute the entire effect to existence? Because existence as unrestricted does not, by itself and as unqualified, account for the variety of its concrete appearances. Considered in its unity, the effusion is one; its differentiation depends on the ranks. Their rulings appear in every effusion that relates to them. The relation called 'contact' is not a physical collision. It is the effect's becoming determined at a rank, according to that rank's capacity. An effusion that **arrives and remains** at a rank is conditioned in one manner, whereas an effusion **passing through** it toward another rank is conditioned in another manner. These differences account for why ranks may have an effect even when a disclosure is not arrested within them.

Nor is it enough to give this efficacy exclusively to the rulings of necessity and possibility. Those rulings do not stand alone; they have to be established under the ranks. The resulting causal account therefore considers the intelligible ranks together with the relevant divine and possible rulings. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** The ranks are like relative endpoints when one considers the course of essential effusion and existential self-disclosure through the stations and degrees determined between eternity without beginning and eternity without end—without a final goal or fixed resting-place.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers an objection. If ranks influence effusion only when effusion reaches and is determined at them, how can they condition what merely passes through them? Because each rank is a **relative limit** in relation to a disclosure's course, whether the disclosure remains there or continues through it. The commentary continues on p. 174.

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** A rank may serve as the relative endpoint for the effusion that sustains its own existence through the whole duration allotted to it, as in the case of sanctified spirits. Or it may be a relative endpoint for an effusion that passes onward to other ranks. Even where the special share proper to that rank does not leave it, the effusion proceeds through it toward things below it in rank and acts upon them. For that reason every rank is a relative destination: at each, what reaches it becomes determinate according to its capacity.

The ranks are relative endpoints by reference to the journey of essential effusion, that is, existential self-disclosure, through successive stations and degrees. The term *stations* may be applied to those points from which the effusion moves altogether to another place; *degrees* to the remaining differences of order, including those in which a disclosure endures while another proceeds. The series is situated between what is without beginning and what is without end, yet there is no last goal beyond which nothing remains, and no absolute cessation at the point already reached. New creation (*khalq jadīd*) is constantly realized across the instances of manifestation. Movement is treated here as an affirmative existential event, whereas rest, insofar as it is the sheer negation of movement, is privative. Consequently the course of disclosure is ceaseless. A rank thus counts as the end of what has preceded it, but not as the absolute end of what succeeds it. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** It is now evident from what I have explained that the ranks gather the groups of rulings that stand established within them from the presences of necessity and possibility. They make manifest the results of their conjunction, but according to the ranks themselves—not simply according to the rulings taken alone, nor according to unrestricted effusion alone. Their relation is that of shapes and moulds to things shaped and moulded when these reach and occupy them. This is their efficacy. They are fixed in their intelligible entities; the resulting rulings are traced back to them and ultimately attributed to them, for they are their source and their return. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** A rank gathers the rulings of necessity and possibility that apply to it, and these remain established relative to it, even if a particular effusion passes away from it or affects something else through it. The rulings arise from the divine and necessary names and from the names connected with the possible realm, whose respective presences abide. Accordingly the rulings derived from them also have a stable intelligible place.

The ranks manifest the results produced by the conjunction of the two orders of rulings. This is clarified by comparing a rank with a shape or mould: the arriving effusion receives a determinate form, while the mould, under the relevant consideration, stays as it is. [Continued p. 175.]

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If some ranks arise from others, there must be a fitting relationship between what precedes and what follows, such that the subsequent rank is connected with its predecessor.

**Qūnawī:** A chapter on connection.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, on the connection of certain divine names with others, whereby some arise from and are ordered after others.

**Qūnawī:** The secret of affinities (*munāsabāt*) lies in sharing something that removes the rulings of mutual otherness under the aspect in which affinity is established.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The reason that two things can be suitably related is that they share an aspect in virtue of which the differentiation between them is set aside—though in another respect they remain different, so that one can precede the other and the other follow it. Affinity (*munāsaba*) may be **intrinsic** (*dhātiyya*) or a matter of **rank** (*martabiyya*). Intrinsic affinity occurs between the Real and the human being, or between human individuals; rank-based affinity is here treated among human individuals. The two kinds must not be confused.

**Qūnawī:** The first and highest is intrinsic affinity. Between the Real and the human being—who is the intended locus—it is established in two ways. The first concerns the weakness of the effect of the human being as a mirror upon the self-disclosure determined in that mirror, so that it does not give the disclosure a qualification incompatible with divine transcendence, beyond the necessary qualification of determination. That qualification does not impugn the greatness, majesty and oneness of the Real. This also involves freedom from most of the rulings of possibility and from the properties of intervening mediations. The different degrees of the ones brought near and of the solitary perfected ones derive from this aspect.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Intrinsic affinity comes first because it concerns the highest and earliest ranks of manifestation. Among loci it belongs in the fullest sense to the human being, and especially to the perfect human, who is the intended end of manifestation. One aspect of this affinity is negative or privative: the mirror's own fixed reality exerts the least possible limitation on the self-disclosure that appears within it. The less the mirror's individual properties distort the disclosure, the more closely the appearance resembles its source under the aspect of transcendence. Yet a created mirror cannot be altogether without an effect, for what appears in it necessarily has the determination of appearing in *this* mirror rather than another.

Under strict comparison, even that determination is less than the unrestricted Reality. The image is a shadow and cannot equal that whose shadow it is; a determinate shadow cannot encompass the majesty of its source; and determination as distinct from its source implies a relative duality. For these reasons Qūnawī speaks of the **weakness** of the mirror's conditioning action, rather than its complete absence. The difficulty is only resolved when determinate manifestation is not confused with the Essence considered in itself. The same negative affinity comes from the high rank's relative freedom from possible limitations and from intermediary properties. Proximity to the Real means that the rulings of necessity are more evident and the limitations of possibility less evident in the manifestation. [Continued p. 178.]

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The perfected individual exhibits the first affinity, because the mirror's conditioning action is slight and the limitations of possibility are diminished. He also gathers the second affinity, because the possible manifestations of divine attributes and of the cosmic ranks are comprehended in him. He is called the *isthmus of isthmuses* because he joins, in a higher and more inclusive way, what less comprehensive intermediary ranks join only under limited aspects. Other isthmuses mediate necessity and possibility or spirits and bodies. Hence the perfected human possesses the most encompassing created knowledge of the Real through the disclosure of these aspects in him.

The end of creation, in this account, is the manifestation of this comprehensiveness, joining synthesis and detail. The person who possesses only the first mode may be beloved because of purity and proximity and may resemble the divine in having fewer possible limitations; nevertheless, without gathering the relevant whole, he does not have the fully intended comprehensive station. **Qūnawī (continuing):** ...receives a more noble and elevated spirit in relation to the ranks of the higher intellects and souls. A temperament further from the point of equilibrium receives what corresponds to a lower rank and a lesser measure of nobility.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Intrinsic affinity between human beings has two aspects analogous to the divine–human case. The first is a relative absence of dissimilarity in the constitution: the two persons may occupy one degree among the different degrees of balance proper to the human species, or neighbouring degrees with no intermediate degree between them. Each class of generated things—mineral, vegetable, animal and human—has its distinctive constitution; each species within a class, each subgroup, and each individual also has its proper constitution. If the constitution required for a species disappears, that kind of individual cannot persist. The species-wide temperament thus comprehends a range of variations in individual and subgroup temperaments, and similarity or adjacency within this range establishes the relevant affinity.

This affinity has special significance, says the commentator, for the relation of spiritual pupils to masters, for their capacity to benefit one another, and for the attraction of one to another. The connection is not commonly understood even experientially among guides. For human spirits become individually determined from spiritual ranks—the intellects and souls—and are differentiated in nobility according to the greater or lesser interposition of other ranks. Fewer and weaker intermediaries mean that the rulings of possibility are less numerous and more attenuated. More powerful or more numerous mediations mean stronger and more numerous limitations. After God's decree, the mixture's degree of equilibrium conditions the manner in which a spirit is determined and manifested in the embodied person.

A temperament in which the opposed elemental tendencies are more completely harmonized approximates unity, and is therefore suited to receiving a nobler spirit. The closest approach to true equilibrium is described as the centre of the circle within which perfect souls are determined, a point at which the elemental tendencies are brought into complete balance. Al-Mahāʾimī marks this as differing from some philosophers' account of equilibrium. The spirit is received according to that degree of suitability, whether it derives, in the cosmology assumed here, from the intellects or from the higher souls. A temperament further removed from the centre corresponds to a lower degree of spiritual manifestation. [Continued p. 181.]

قال المصنف رضي اللّه عنه : [ فتعرف حالة إذ ] أي : حالة إذ يعرف ما ذكرنا عن شهود ، أو فهم محقق إن الشرط الأكبر قيد به ؛ لأن لهذا التفاوت شرطا آخر من الأدوار الفلكية ، وخواص الأمكنة أحوال الأبوين لتفاوت أرواح الناس في الشرف والخسة ، هو قرب الأمزجة من نقطة الاعتدال الحقيقي وبعدها عنها ، 
لكن ذلك بعد سابق علم اللّه المسمى بالعناية والقضاء والمشيئة ، جعله بعدها ؛ لأنه أثر المزاج الذي هو أثر العناية التي هي المشيئة ؛ لأن أثرها يختص بحسب التسوية الربانية المسماة الاعتدال ، ربانية لحصولها من الرتبة الإلهية ، يليها نفخ الروح الذي هو تعين الروح لما فيه من الخروج من مقامه الغيبي إلى الظهور الذي هو التعين.
 
فلذلك قال : [ فافهم ] ، وإنما قال : وتذكر لتعرف بذلك التناسب الذّاتي من الوجه الآخر ، وذلك باستجماع خواص تلك الملائكة ، وعينه . 

قال الشيخ رضي اللّه عنه : [ وأما المناسبة المرتبية ، فإنها ليست من وجه واحد ، بل من وجوه متعددة : أحدها من جهة معدنها الأصلية التي هي مبدأ تعينات الأرواح المشار إليها آنفا ،

**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...the original sources from which spirits are determined. The source of the highest of them, that is, the spirits of the perfected, is the Mother of the Book (*umm al-kitāb*). The first determination of certain others, in knowledge and in an existence comprehended under unity, is the reality of the Supreme Pen, called the First Intellect and Universal Spirit. Some are determined from the Preserved Tablet, others from the spirituality of the Throne associated with Isrāfīl, some from the spirituality of the Footstool associated with Mīkāʾīl, and others from the rank of Jibrīl at the Lote Tree. This ordering continues down through the types of these spiritual principles to the lowest heaven, whose spiritual chief Ismāʿīl corresponds to what the Peripatetic philosophers call the Active Intellect.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In treating rank-based affinities, Qūnawī chooses three of their many possible aspects: the source from which the ranks begin, their mode or locus of appearance, and the intermediate stage connecting those beginnings with their manifestations. The first aspect therefore concerns the original *mines* or sources of spirits, not their subsequent perfection. He had previously distinguished the beginning of a spirit's determination from the station at which it becomes complete.

The perfected human spirits—those of prophets, poles and solitary realized individuals—begin from the Mother of the Book, explained here as divine knowledge in its comprehensive rather than differentiated consideration. It is the origin of origins in relation to the intellect and soul, themselves called divine books in the language of this cosmology. The *book* can also signify the great cosmos, whose intelligible principle is knowledge. The beings determined through the Supreme Pen or First Intellect receive a more unfolded mode of determination, one actually distinguished from what is below it while still united by comparison with subordinate ranks. The Pen is so called because of the image of writing and inscription; it is Intellect as comprehending things intelligibly and Universal Spirit as a principle to which lesser spiritual determinations are related.

Other spirits belong to the Tablet, to the Throne and its spiritual orders, to the Footstool, to the Lote Tree, and to further angelic and celestial ranks. Qūnawī's invocation of the Active Intellect at the lowest heaven is intended to bring the hierarchical account into comparison with the philosophers. Al-Mahāʾimī disputes the view that the Active Intellect's action is simply confined to the elemental world. The references to the Peripatetics here belong to a medieval reconstruction of philosophical lineage and cosmology, not to an independently established history of Aristotle and Plato. He then explains that the source of the determination of the highest spirits—the spirits of the perfected, among prophets, poles and solitary individuals—is the Mother of the Book, namely comprehensive divine knowledge. It is so called because it is the origin of origins for intellects and soul, which are divine books: the “book” here means the great cosmos, and knowledge is its origin. The determination of some begins in a differentiated manner under one aspect of their existence, while being comprehensive under another. This unity is relative to what lies beneath it. Existence here is actual, unlike at the first rank. Its source is the reality of the Supreme Pen itself, without the Preserved Tablet's relation to it. It is called Pen because through it the cosmos is recorded and inscribed; Intellect because it first understands the whole, being first in rank among creatures; Spirit because through it the cosmos is governed; and Universal because the universal spirits are its particulars. **Qūnawī:** Another aspect of affinity is through the spirits' imaginal loci of manifestation. Spirits, despite their unequal ranks, are never without the loci through which they become determined and appear, according to all the realized knowers. The first rank in which human spirits appear, apart from the perfected, is the **absolute imaginal world** (*ʿālam al-mithāl al-muṭlaq*).

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This is the second aspect among the selected kinds of rank-based affinity. It concerns the starting-point of outward appearance, rather than the original spiritual source considered in itself. The absolute imaginal world is the realm in which spirits may appear through perceptible forms without gross bodies and without requiring the particular faculty of imagination lodged in an individual person's brain. Such forms make distinct appearances possible without reducing the spirit to elemental matter.

The commentator offers a philosophical argument: spirits, considered without any manifesting loci, are simple realities. If they were all of one specific kind without a way of acquiring determinate forms, their differences would not be enough to distinguish individuals as individuals. Merely appealing to different ranks would not fully resolve the problem, because a rank is a general condition rather than the particular determination of an individual. Individual characteristics do not become actual externally before manifestation. The imaginal loci provide the level at which distinct appearances become intelligible and visible. Apart from the perfected human spirits, which are treated as having a higher mode of determination, human spirits first acquire such manifestations in the absolute imaginal world. The commentator refers to Ibn ʿArabī's *ʿUqlat al-mustawfiz* for a corresponding cosmographical account.

**Qūnawī:** Imaginal forms may take their originating material from the subtleties of the powers of this natural life and from its purified and refined substances clothed in the qualities of spirits. Yet their descriptions and states in Paradise are manifested according to their spiritualities and powers and according to the properties of their imaginal loci.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This indicates that the imaginal world both supplies and receives the loci through which the spirits of the people of Paradise appear. The natural human faculties involved are the animal powers, including outer and inner senses, and the vegetative faculties, as these are refined by righteous acts and noble character. The heart and the soul likewise contribute their refined subtleties, insofar as the heart is purified of domination by the commanding lower soul and the soul is refined in its traits. [Continued p. 185.]

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The heart and soul, once purified and made suitable, acquire qualities corresponding to spiritual forms. The forms found in Paradise are related to them; yet the specific qualities and changes of those forms in Paradise are not merely the direct persistence of earthly matter. They manifest according to the powers of the spirits and the properties of their imaginal bodies. Their capacity to change without the generation and corruption that characterize elemental bodies is adduced as evidence that the relevant level is the imaginal realm. In this way the imaginal world is both the place to which the outward forms of spirits are referred and the source from which they become manifest.

**Qūnawī:** The dwellings of the people of Paradise are manifestations of the ranks of their spirits, both in respect of those spirits' standing before the Real and in respect of their first imaginal loci. The Prophet indicated this through subtle allusions, as when he is reported to have said to ʿAlī that his palace in Paradise would be opposite, or alongside, the Prophet's palace, and similarly concerning al-ʿAbbās. He also spoke of the people of faith as recognizing their dwellings in Paradise more readily than they recognize their homes in this world. This is a consequence of affinity.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The dwellings themselves therefore participate in the imaginal differentiation of the inhabitants: the purer or more attenuated the imaginal locus, the more appropriate its dwelling, without requiring the outward position of the dwelling to correspond identically to its occupant's spiritual station. The distinction matters in the report about ʿAlī's palace being opposite the Prophet's. The Prophet's spiritual rank exceeds that of even the highest saints. Mere physical or imaginal adjacency does not imply equality or near equality of spiritual station. The comparable statement about al-ʿAbbās makes this even clearer. Proximity in the configuration of a dwelling is one kind of relation, proximity in spiritual rank another. Qūnawī calls the reports subtle indications for precisely this reason.

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The robes and gifts are described as coming 'from the Real' precisely to distinguish them from the forms generated under the ordinary imaginal channels. The people brought to the mound of vision need a renewed suitability (*istiʿdād*). If a standing suitability alone sufficed for continued vision, there would be no need for a new gift or periodic entrance. Such vision requires an affinity proper to the divine Essence and its names. The direct intrinsic affinity is not acquired by the servant as an autonomous property; it is mediated through the divine names and attributes that possess a particular lordship in relation to each servant. The gifts awaken or renew the delicate ties (*raqāʾiq*) binding them to those names, thereby strengthening the relation that permits their entrance to the station of visitation.

**Qūnawī:** The divine command to the angels at the conclusion of the inhabitants' assemblies of visitation, 'Return them to their palaces,' indicates that the rulings of the affinities supplied by these gifts and robes have reached their limit. The names and attributes which, under their particular operation, established an affinity of proximity and gathering have completed their rule. When the sovereignty of other names and attributes, opposed to those which occasion gathering, becomes manifest, the rulings that distinguish and separate prevail; consequently distance and veiling occur. **Al-Mahāʾimī:** The command to return the visitors demonstrates that the special affinity occasioned by the gifts depends on the operative rulings of names and attributes. If it were a permanent condition independent of those rulings, the vision would not come to an end. The termination of the visitation indicates the termination of the particular conjunction that made it possible. This is not a claim that God changes essentially: what changes is the operative relationship of distinct names to determinate recipients. The following explanation develops their alternation. الحق ، فلا يستحقون به الحمل إلى كثيب الرؤية لزيارة الحق ومجالسته ، فهي مظاهر أحكام الأسماء والصفات التي استندا في الواقع إليها ، وإن لم يعلموا استنادهم إليها إلى الآن ، ثم ذكر فائدة إتيان الملائكة بها ، بأنه لا بد لهم من حصول استعداد جديد ، إذ المستمر لو كان كافيا لمراتب الرؤية بدوامه ؛ على أن الرؤيا تحتاج إلى مناسبة ذاتية وأسمائية ، لكن المناسبة بالذات لا تحصل بنفسه إذ لا علاقة بينهما ، بل بواسطة الأسماء والصفات التي لها ربوبية خاصة على أولئك الزائرين ، فبتلك التحف يحيي الرقائق ، أي : تعلقات ارتباطهم بالحق ، فإذا حييت تلك الرقائق ، قربت المناسبة مع الحق ، فصارت من جهة الذات والأسماء جميعا تستحق الحمل إلى كثيب الرؤية . 

قال رضي اللّه عنه : [ وقوله تعالى للملائكة في أواخر مجالس الزيارة عن أهل الجنة ردوهم إلى قصورهم ، إشارة إلى انتهاء أحكام المناسبات المستفادة من تلك الخلع والتحف ، وانتهاء أحكام الأسماء والصفات التي هي من حيث هي تثبت المناسبة بينهم وبين الحق ، ويوجب جميعهم وحضورهم عنده ، فمتى ظهرت سلطنة الأسماء والصفات التي تقابل أحكام الأسماء والصفات المقتضية للاجتماع ، ظهرت الأحكام القاضية بالامتياز ، فحصل البعد والحجاب ، فافهم ] . 

إشارة إلى الاستدلال على أنها مظاهر أحكام الأسماء والصفات ، وإلا لم تنقطع المناسبة المستفادة من تلك الخلع والتحف بانقطاع أحكام تلك الأسماء التي تثبت المناسبة بين الزائرين وبين الحق ، لكن المناسبة تنقطع بدليل انقطاع موجبها من الرؤية عند الرد إلى القصور ، مع أن المعلول واجب من العلة ، 

فالعلة التي هي المناسبة منقطعة ، فلا بدّ من انقطاع علة المناسبة أيضا ، وهي أحكام الأسماء والصفات المقابلة لتلك الأسماء والصفات ، على أولئك الزائرين بحيث صارت أربابهم بعد ما كانت الربوبية أولا لتلك الأسماء السابقة في المقابلة ، 

وتلك السلطنة أحكام تلك الأسماء السابقة المقتضية للاجتماع ، فمتى ظهرت سلطنة هذه الأسماء ظهرت الأحكام القاضية بالامتياز بين أولئك الزائرين وبين الحق ، فحصل البعد فيما بينهما وحصل الحجاب وهكذا انتهت سلطنة هذه الأسماء المقتضية للبعد والحجاب ، وانتهت أحكامها ، عادت سلطنة الأسماء الأول ، فعادوا إلى الرؤية ، فعلم أن لكل اسم حدّا معلوما في السلطنة محلا وزمانا ، فلها الربوبية بحسب تلك

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The relational cause of gathering is the reign of the divine names that bring the visitors near. When their special rulings give way to the complementary rulings of names that establish distinction, the recipients experience separation and a veil from the specific station of vision. They are returned to their dwellings. When the reign of those distinguishing names in turn reaches its end, the names giving rise to gathering again become operative, and the visitors are admitted once more. Every divine name thus has a known scope for its particular rulings and sovereignty, in relation to a place of manifestation and an interval appropriate to that rank. Its lordship is exercised in accordance with those determinate conditions and their order, not as an exclusive power separate from the Essence. This is the sense in which the ruler of a given manifestation changes without any implication of an intrinsically changing divine Essence.

**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** ...times.

**Qūnawī:** As for the differences of their ranks while sitting with the Real, these accord with their differing ranks in the Real Himself, and with the soundness of their beliefs concerning God, or their sound knowledge and witnessing, and their earlier preference for the presence of the Real over everything else. The length or brevity of the audience, the differing honour of what is addressed to them, and what they understand of His address accord with what we have mentioned. They also accord with their presence to what they knew of Him, or their calling Him to mind according to their beliefs concerning Him; their affinity with His presence in respect of the station of the mound of vision; and the self-disclosure from Him particular to them. Know this.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This indicates what appears to them according to intrinsic affinity, after describing what appears according to affinity through names. Although all share in affinity, their differing degrees of proximity to and distance from the Real accord with their ranks in the Real Himself. Intrinsic affinity differs in degree, whether in respect of the weakness of the effect of the servant's rank upon the determined divine self-disclosure, or in respect of the servant's share in the form of divine comprehensiveness. It also accords with the soundness of their beliefs concerning God. These too yield intrinsic affinity, to the point of entailing annihilation in Him and subsistence through Him.

By specifying soundness he excludes corrupt beliefs, which entail distance and veiling. This concerns the complete. Their previous preference—that is, before being carried to the mound of vision—for the Real's presence over all else also yields intrinsic affinity through love of Him, until the person becomes a manifestation of eternal love and it appears therein in its fullness or in some measure. This applies both to the complete and to others.

He then explains that the length or brevity of the audience accords with the aforementioned ranks in the Real Himself; soundness of beliefs, knowledge and witnessing; and preference for the Real's presence. It also accords with their presence to Him in this world and their calling Him to mind according to their beliefs, and with their affinity to His presence through the names which brought them to the station of the mound of vision and bestowed the self-disclosure particular to them. The factors mentioned first entail only the audience itself, with a certain measure of nearness or distance. The differing honour of what they are addressed with and what they understand follows the same pattern, even though the address is one.
